RagShortTexts: Grain stores need dry roofs, sound walls and rodent checks; cats provide only part of care.
Losses to rent grain and seed affect estates and homes beyond the recorded intake.

Variants.Content:
Stored grain remains vulnerable to rats, mice and damp. Rodents enter cracks and holes, while a leaking roof spoils a corner of the stock. Raised dry floors, sound covers and containers need maintenance, and spilled grain at doors needs clearing. Cats hunt around homes and stores but do not mend holes, move wet sacks or identify spoiled grain.

Stocks must be divided among eating, seed, dues and promised loans, with inspections reaching below the surface. Losses accumulate quietly; discovering a shortage in spring may force borrowing or smaller sowings. Keys, access and observed movements can cause disputes over whether grain was issued or stolen. Reliable handovers matter more than counting bags alone.
Storekeepers must report condition and available shares. Keeping a cat does not account for leaks and holes; owners still need repair workers and materials.
Troops inspect sack bottoms for damp clumps and mend bags that spill in transit. An unattended store risks both rations and trust in distribution.
Poor households feel even small losses. Cats also need care while roofs and vessels need checking; a seed shortage can mean borrowing from kin.
